title: Short Stuff: Rhodium
summary: Short Stuff episode on rhodium. Josh and Chuck open with a dramatized Christmas Eve 1800 scene of William Hyde Wallaston and Smithson Tennant buying a platinum nugget from Nueva Granada (Colombia), then cover how the two chemists isolated rhodium and palladium from leftover reddish salts, and how rhodium got its name from the Greek word for rose. They discuss rhodium as a platinum group / noble metal, its rarity, and its price peaking near $30,000 an ounce in April 2021 before falling to around $4,000. Demand fell largely because catalytic converters, which use rhodium to convert nitrous oxide emissions, are declining with electric vehicles. They cover main sources (South Africa about 80 percent, then Russia and Zimbabwe), rhodium plating of jewelry (shiny, hard, hypoallergenic, but its fumes are harmful), and its use as a catalyst in menthol production. The episode ends with a sign-off.
topics: electric vehicles and precious metal demand

segments.title: Opening scene: Christmas Eve 1800
segments.summary: Hosts open with a dramatized scene of Wallaston and Tennant buying platinum in 1800.

segments.title: Platinum purchase and discovery of rhodium
segments.summary: The pair bought a platinum nugget from Nueva Granada for about 795 pounds, smuggled it out, and worked on making platinum malleable. Leftover reddish salts led them to discover rhodium and palladium.

segments.title: Name origin and platinum group metals
segments.summary: Rhodium is named after the Greek word for rose because its salts are reddish. It belongs to the platinum group metals and noble metals alongside iridium, ruthenium, platinum, palladium, and osmium.

segments.title: Rarity and price peak
segments.summary: Rhodium is rare, almost never found in pure form, and was extremely expensive, peaking near $30,000 an ounce in April 2021 before falling to around $4,000.

segments.title: Demand decline and catalytic converters
segments.summary: Demand fell as electric vehicles reduce reliance on catalytic converters, which use rhodium to convert nitrous oxide emissions. Catalytic converter theft is also tied to the metals they contain.
topics: electric vehicles and precious metal demand

segments.title: Sources and jewelry plating
segments.summary: South Africa produces about 80 percent of rhodium, followed by Russia and Zimbabwe, mostly as a byproduct of platinum mines, including one in Montana. Rhodium is shiny, hard, and hypoallergenic, and is used to plate jewelry, though dissolving it releases harmful fumes.

segments.title: Plating durability and menthol catalyst
segments.summary: Rhodium plating is scratch and corrosion resistant but wears down, so it may need replating every few years, and only a tiny amount is needed. Rhodium is also the catalyst in the reaction that produces menthol.

segments.title: Tangents and sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts discuss whether menthol cigarettes are being phased out, a personal dream tangent, and close out the Short Stuff episode.
